# Lab 5: Getting started

**Exploratory Data Analysis with pandas, NumPy and scikit-learn**
Data Handling and Infrastructure for AI | MSc | 2-hour lab

> [!NOTE]
> **Read this first.** The lab is ten short tasks. Most of the code is already written: you fill in a few blanks, and a check cell tells you whether your number is right.
>
> If something goes wrong, do not worry: almost every problem has a simple fix, and they are all in [section 5](#5-what-to-do-when-something-goes-wrong) and [section 6](#6-quick-tips-for-each-task).

## Contents

1. [What you need](#1-what-you-need)
2. [Open the notebook in Google Colab](#2-open-the-notebook-in-google-colab)
3. [How to run the notebook](#3-how-to-run-the-notebook)
4. [How each task works](#4-how-each-task-works)
5. [What to do when something goes wrong](#5-what-to-do-when-something-goes-wrong)
6. [Quick tips for each task](#6-quick-tips-for-each-task)
7. [How to ask for help](#7-how-to-ask-for-help)
8. [Before you leave](#8-before-you-leave)


---

## 1. What you need

- A web browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari) and a Google account. You do not need to install anything.
- The notebook file `Lab5_EDA.ipynb` 

---

## 2. Open the notebook in Google Colab

**Quickest way (from GitHub):** click the button below.

[Open Lab 5 in Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/SETU-AIML-2026/DH-Infra-AI/blob/main/topic-03-sprint-2-weeks-4-6/unit-4-week-5-lab/notebook-1-week-5-eda/Lab5_EDA.ipynb)


**Other ways to open it:**

1. Go to [colab.research.google.com](https://colab.research.google.com) and sign in with your Google account.
2. In the window that opens, choose the **GitHub** tab and paste the repository address, **or** choose **Upload** and select `Lab5_EDA.ipynb`. (If the window does not appear: **File > Upload notebook**.)
3. Alternatively, upload the file to Google Drive, right-click it and choose **Open with > Google Colaboratory**.
4. Wait a few seconds. You should see the title **Lab 5: Exploratory Data Analysis...** and the plan table.
5. **Immediately** choose **File > Save a copy in Drive**, so that your work is saved under your own account. (Changes you make are not saved to the repository, so without your own copy your work is lost when the session ends.)

---

## 3. How to run the notebook

A notebook is made of **cells**. Text cells explain; code cells contain Python that you run.

| To do this | Do this |
|---|---|
| **Run one code cell** | Click the cell, then press the play button on its left, or press `Shift + Enter` (runs and moves on) or `Ctrl + Enter` (runs and stays). |
| **Run the cells above this one** | **Runtime > Run before**. Use this if you get an error saying something is "not defined". |
| **Edit a text cell** (written answers) | Double-click it, type, then press `Shift + Enter` to close it. |
| **Insert or delete a cell** | Hover between cells and click **+ Code**; to delete, use the bin icon at the top right of the cell. |
| **Undo** | `Ctrl + Z` (`Cmd + Z` on a Mac). |
| **Stop a cell that is running** | **Runtime > Interrupt execution**. |
| **Start again cleanly** | **Runtime > Restart session**, then run the Setup cells and the cells you need. |

The first time you run a cell, Colab connects to a computer in the cloud. This can take 10 to 20 seconds: wait for the cell to finish (the play button stops spinning).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Golden rule: run cells in order, from top to bottom.** Each cell uses results from the cells above it. If you skip one, later cells will say that something is "not defined".

---

## 4. How each task works

Every task has the same shape, so after Task 1 you will know what to expect.

- **A short explanation** and the lecture slide numbers where you saw the pattern.
- **A code cell with blanks.** A blank looks like `___` (three underscores). Replace each one with your answer. Until you do, you will see a red error: `NameError: name '___' is not defined`. This is expected, not a mistake.
- **A hint** (click "Hint" to open it). Try for two minutes first.
- **A check cell.** `PASS` means your number is right. `CHECK AGAIN` means re-read your blanks. A pass tells you the number is right, not that your explanation is.
- **Sometimes a short written answer** (one or two sentences, in your own words). The reasoning matters more than the code.

**Example of a blank**

Before:

```python
"Survived is 0 or 1":      ___,
```

After (the pattern is on slide 12):

```python
"Survived is 0 or 1":      set(frame["Survived"]) <= {0, 1},
```

---

## 5. What to do when something goes wrong

### Step 1: read the error from the bottom

Python errors are long, but the useful part is the **last line**. Read the last line first; it names the problem. Then look for the arrow (`---->`) that shows which line caused it.

```text
NameError                          Traceback (most recent call last)
/tmp/ipython-input-12.py in <cell line: 0>()
      3     "Survived is 0 or 1": ___,
----> 4     "Pclass is 1, 2 or 3": ___,
NameError: name '___' is not defined          <-- read this line first
```

| Error name | What it usually means |
|---|---|
| `NameError` | Python does not know that name. Either a blank (`___`) is still there, you misspelled a variable, or you did not run an earlier cell (use **Runtime > Run before**). |
| `KeyError` | A column name is misspelled. Names are case-sensitive: `"Pclass"` is not `"pclass"`. |
| `SyntaxError` | A typo in the code: a missing quote, bracket or comma. Look at the line with the arrow and the line just above it. |
| `TypeError` | The wrong kind of thing was used, for example a list where a number was expected, or a missing argument. |
| `ValueError` | The right kind of thing but a wrong value or shape, for example an array of the wrong length. |
| `AttributeError` | You used `.something` that does not exist for that object. Check the spelling: `.isna()`, `.mean()`, `.to_numpy()`. |

### Step 2: look up your problem

| What you see | Why it happens | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `NameError: name '___' is not defined` | A blank is not filled in yet. | Replace `___` with your answer. This error is normal until you do. |
| `NameError: name 'df'` (or `'X_train'`, `'model'`, ...) `is not defined` | An earlier cell was not run, or the session restarted. | **Runtime > Run before** (on the cell with the error), then run it again. Cells with unfilled blanks above will show errors: fill them in. |
| `URLError`, `HTTPError`, or "Could not download" when loading the data | The network is blocking GitHub, or the internet dropped. | Upload `titanic.csv`: click the **folder icon** on the left, then the **upload icon**, and choose the file. Re-run the load cell (it falls back to `titanic.csv` automatically). |
| `CHECK AGAIN` | Your number is different from the expected one. | Re-read the blanks. Open the hint. Compare with the slide. Check quotes, brackets and the right data (`X_train`, not `X`). |
| Your number is slightly different from a neighbour's or the slide's | A different `random_state`, rounding, or a different split. | Use the exact values the task gives (for example `test_size=0.2`, `random_state=42`). The checks allow small rounding differences. |
| Red or pink text starting with `FutureWarning` or `UserWarning` | A warning, not an error. | Ignore it. The cell worked. |
| A cell has been running for a long time | Task 8 is the slowest. | Task 8 takes 5 to 15 seconds. If any cell runs for more than a minute, use **Runtime > Interrupt execution** and re-run it once. |
| The plot does not appear | The cell was interrupted, or has an error above the plot. | Run the cell again and read the last line of any error. |
| "Session crashed", "Runtime disconnected", or all your variables are gone | Colab disconnects after being idle, or memory ran out. | Click **Reconnect**. Then **Runtime > Restart session**, run the Setup cells, and use **Runtime > Run before** to get back to your task. |
| You deleted or broke a cell that was provided | Easy to do by accident. | Press `Ctrl + Z` straight away. Otherwise copy your blanks somewhere, re-open a fresh copy of the notebook and paste them back. |
| dtype shows `str` in one place and `object` in another | Different versions of pandas. | Ignore it. The two behave the same here. |
| A text cell shows symbols like `$$` or `\frac` | A formula that did not render. | Ignore it. It is only the formula. |
| You cannot sign in to Google | Some institutional accounts block Colab. | Use a personal Google account, or ask your lecturer for help. |

---

## 6. Quick tips for each task

| Task | Things that often trip people up |
|---|---|
| **1** | Use curly brackets `{ }` for the set of allowed values. Copy the pattern from slide 12 and only change the column and the values. |
| **2** | Use `.isna()` and then `.mean() * 100`, rounded to 1 decimal place. The two blanks in `assign()` are True/False columns (for Age and for Cabin). |
| **3** | The fence is Q3 + 1.5 x (Q3 - Q1): subtract the quartiles. For the share, divide by *all* first-class passengers (216), not by 891. |
| **4** | Use `dropna()` before sorting. The ranks start at 1, so the last ECDF value is exactly 1. |
| **5** | Cramér's V needs brackets: `np.sqrt(chi2 / (n * k))`. The method name goes in quotes: `method="wilson"`. |
| **6** | `"size"` and `"mean"` need quotes. The overall rate is total admitted divided by total applied, not the average of the department rates. |
| **7** | Give `train_test_split` the features `X` (not the whole `df`). Use the *training* numbers for the test rows. Use `np.nanmean` and `np.nanstd` with `axis=0`. |
| **8** | It takes 5 to 15 seconds. Run it once and wait. The checks only need the leaky score to be well above 0.5 and the pipeline score to be near 0.5. |
| **9** | Strategies and options need quotes: `"median"`, `"most_frequent"`, `"ignore"`. Fit on `X_train` and `y_train`; score on `X_test` and `y_test`. |
| **10** | Pass the whole `model` and the raw `X` and `y` to `cross_val_score`, not a transformed matrix. In your own finding row, include a number, an action and a limitation. |

---

## 7. How to ask for help

1. Read the last line of the error and try the table above.
2. Ask your fellow students/colleagues. Explaining where you are stuck often finds the problem.
3. Drop a text in Slack. Tell us which task you are on and show the last two or three lines of the error.

It is fine to ask. Nobody is expected to finish with every blank perfect: the goal is to understand each step.

---

## 8. Before you leave

1. Check that the cells you have done show `PASS` (or ask about the ones that do not).
2. Use **File > Save a copy in Drive** if you have not already. To keep a copy on your computer: **File > Download > Download .ipynb**.
3. That is all. **There is nothing to hand in and no homework from this lab.**

**Colab not available?** You can run the notebook on your own computer with Jupyter. Install the packages once with:

```bash
pip install pandas numpy matplotlib seaborn scipy scikit-learn statsmodels jupyter
```

then start Jupyter (`jupyter notebook`) and open the same file. Ask your lecturer if you need help.

# Lab 5: Exploratory Data Analysis with pandas, NumPy and scikit-learn
**Data Handling and Infrastructure for AI | MSc | 2 hours**

### How this notebook works
* Run the cells **in order, from top to bottom**.
* Most code is already written. In each task you complete **a few blanks marked `___`** (until you do, you will see a `NameError`: that is expected).
* After each task a **self-check** cell prints `PASS` or `CHECK AGAIN`. If you see `CHECK AGAIN`, re-read your blanks. Use the hint if you are stuck, or just ask.
* Some tasks end with a **short written answer** (one or two sentences, double-click the cell to edit). Write in your own words.

## Setup
Run the two cells below, one after the other. The first imports everything and defines `check`. The second loads the data and keeps an untouched copy, `df_raw`.

# --- Setup: run once ---------------------------------------------------------
import warnings
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import scipy.stats as st

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, classification_report
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=FutureWarning)
pd.set_option("display.width", 140)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 30)
pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", 110)
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"] = (7, 3.4)

def check(label, ok):
    """Self-check: prints PASS or CHECK AGAIN."""
    print(("PASS         " if bool(ok) else "CHECK AGAIN  ") + label)

# --- Load the data (provided) --------------------------------------------------
URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datasciencedojo/datasets/master/titanic.csv"
try:
    df = pd.read_csv(URL)
except Exception:
    # If the download is blocked: upload titanic.csv with the file panel on the left, then:
    df = pd.read_csv("titanic.csv")

df_raw = df.copy()        # untouched copy
print("shape:", df.shape)
df.head(3)

## Task 1. Write a data contract
A **data contract** is code that states what the data *should* look like, so that you find out immediately if it ever stops being true.  For example `set(df["Survived"]) <= {0, 1}`.

Complete the three blanks, using the same pattern. (`PassengerId` is done for you.)

check("the real file satisfies the contract", all(contract(df).values()))

# Now we corrupt a COPY on purpose and see whether the contract notices (provided):
bad = df.copy()
bad.loc[0, "Pclass"] = 4
print(contract(bad))
check("the contract catches the corrupted copy", not all(contract(bad).values()))

## Task 2. How much is missing, and for whom?
**Measure before you decide.** First, the percentage of missing values per column. Then, the missing rate of `Age` and `Cabin` **for each passenger class** (the groupby pattern from slide 17: the mean of a True/False column is a proportion).

**Part A.** Fill in the first blank to get the percentage missing per column (rounded to 1 decimal). **Part B.** Fill in the two `isna()` blanks.

missing_pct = ___                 # percent missing per column, rounded to 1 decimal
display(missing_pct[missing_pct > 0].sort_values(ascending=False))

by_class = (
    df.assign(age_na=___, cabin_na=___)
      .groupby("Pclass")[["age_na", "cabin_na"]]
      .mean()
      .round(3)
)
display(by_class)

by_class.mul(100).plot.bar(rot=0, color=["#FF9D38", "#E64141"])
plt.ylabel("% missing"); plt.title("Missing rate by passenger class"); plt.show()

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Part A: `df.isna().mean()` gives the fraction missing for each column; multiply by 100 and use `.round(1)`.
Part B: `df["Age"].isna()` is True where the age is missing.
</details>

check("Cabin 77.1% and Age 19.9% missing", missing_pct["Cabin"] == 77.1 and missing_pct["Age"] == 19.9)
check("Age missing for 27.7% of 3rd class", abs(by_class.loc[3, "age_na"] - 0.277) < 0.002)
check("Cabin missing for 18.5% of 1st class", abs(by_class.loc[1, "cabin_na"] - 0.185) < 0.002)
**Your answer (1 to 2 sentences, double-click to edit).** Look at the plot. Which missingness mechanism (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) does it make *implausible*, and what can you *not* conclude?

## Task 3. Check validity and extreme values
**Part A (just run it).** A validation log: each rule, its rationale, and how many rows break it. Notice the last rule is a *plausibility* check.

**Part B (complete the blanks).** Compute the **1.5 x IQR fence** for `Fare`, count how many passengers it flags, and the **share of all first-class passengers** that would be removed.

# Part A: validation log (provided)
rules = {
    "PassengerId is unique":        ("Row key",                    lambda d: int(d["PassengerId"].duplicated().sum())),
    "Age between 0 and 100":        ("Plausible human range",      lambda d: int((~d["Age"].dropna().between(0, 100)).sum())),
    "Fare is at least 0":           ("Prices cannot be negative",  lambda d: int((d["Fare"] < 0).sum())),
    "Pclass in {1, 2, 3}":          ("Data contract",              lambda d: int((~d["Pclass"].isin([1, 2, 3])).sum())),
    "Fare equals 0 (plausibility)": ("Free passage? crew? unknown", lambda d: int((d["Fare"] == 0).sum())),
}
log = pd.DataFrame([{"rule": k, "rationale": v[0], "violations": v[1](df)} for k, v in rules.items()])
log

# Part B: extreme values
q1, q3 = ___, ___                     # 25th and 75th percentiles of Fare (use .quantile)
fence = ___                           # q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1)
flagged = df[df["Fare"] > fence]
share_first = ___                     # flagged first-class passengers / ALL first-class passengers

print(f"fence = {fence:.1f}; flagged = {len(flagged)} ({len(flagged) / len(df):.0%} of passengers)")
print(f"share of first class flagged: {share_first:.0%}")
print("skewness: raw", round(df["Fare"].skew(), 2), "| after log1p", round(np.log1p(df["Fare"]).skew(), 2))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3))
ax[0].hist(df["Fare"], bins=40, color="#3431B6"); ax[0].axvline(fence, color="#E64141", ls="--"); ax[0].set_title("Fare (raw)")
ax[1].hist(np.log1p(df["Fare"]), bins=40, color="#54B7AF"); ax[1].set_title("log(1 + Fare)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

`q1, q3 = df["Fare"].quantile([0.25, 0.75])`. For the share: count flagged rows where `Pclass == 1`, then divide by the number of rows in the whole data where `Pclass == 1`.
</details>

check("the validation log finds 15 zero fares and no other violations", log["violations"].tolist() == [0, 0, 0, 0, 15])
check("116 passengers flagged", len(flagged) == 116)
check("about 48% of first class flagged", abs(share_first - 0.481) < 0.01)
**Your answer (1 to 2 sentences).** Would you delete the flagged fares? Say why or why not (slides 21 and 22).

## Task 4. The ECDF and the majority baseline
**ECDF** : sort the observed ages, rank them 1 to n, divide by n. The result at any age is the proportion of observed ages at or below it. Remember *n* is 714 (the missing ages are not in it).

**Baseline**: the accuracy of a model that always predicts the most common class. Any real model must beat it.

age = ___                          # the observed ages, sorted, as a NumPy array
ecdf = ___                         # 1/n, 2/n, ..., n/n
plt.step(age, ecdf, where="post", color="#3431B6")
plt.xlabel("Age (years)"); plt.ylabel("Cumulative proportion"); plt.title("ECDF of observed ages"); plt.show()

F28 = (age <= 28).mean()
print("n =", len(age), "| F(28) =", round(F28, 3))

counts = df["Survived"].value_counts()
baseline = ___                     # largest class count divided by the total
print(counts.to_dict(), "| majority baseline accuracy:", round(baseline, 3))

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

`np.sort(df["Age"].dropna().to_numpy())` for the ages; `np.arange(1, len(age) + 1) / len(age)` for the ranks divided by n (the code on slide 26 is the same).
</details>

check("n = 714 observed ages", len(age) == 714)
check("the ECDF reaches exactly 1", ecdf[-1] == 1.0)
check("majority baseline is 0.616", abs(baseline - 549 / 891) < 1e-9)

## Task 5. Compare groups: effect size and uncertainty
**Part A (just run it).** Age by outcome: similar medians, different shapes.

**Part B: Cramer's V**. A p-value only says independence is implausible; **V tells you how strong the association is** (0 to 1): `V = sqrt( chi2 / (n * (min(rows, cols) - 1)) )`. Complete the three blanks.

**Part C: confidence intervals** A rate without its denominator and an interval is an anecdote. Use `proportion_confint` with the **Wilson** method.

# Part A (provided): Age by outcome. Same median, different shape.
display(df.groupby("Survived")["Age"].agg(["count", "mean", "median", "std"]).round(2))
sns.violinplot(data=df, x="Survived", y="Age", inner="quartile", cut=0,
               hue="Survived", palette=["#E64141", "#54B7AF"], legend=False)
plt.title("Age by outcome (survivors include more small children)"); plt.show()

# Part B: Cramer's V
def cramers_v(table):
    chi2, p, dof, _ = st.chi2_contingency(table)
    n = ___                              # total count in the table
    k = ___                              # min(rows, columns) - 1
    return ___                           # the formula for V

t_class = pd.crosstab(df["Pclass"], df["Survived"])
t_sex   = pd.crosstab(df["Sex"], df["Survived"])
print(f"V(Pclass, Survived) = {cramers_v(t_class):.3f}")
print(f"V(Sex, Survived)    = {cramers_v(t_sex):.3f}")

# Part C: Wilson 95% intervals for survival by class
g = df.groupby("Pclass")["Survived"].agg(k="sum", n="size")
g["rate"] = ___                          # k / n
g[["lo", "hi"]] = [proportion_confint(k, n, method=___) for k, n in zip(g["k"], g["n"])]
g.round(3)

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

`n = table.to_numpy().sum()`, `k = min(table.shape) - 1`, and `np.sqrt(chi2 / (n * k))`. For Part C the method name is the string `"wilson"`.
</details>

check("V(Pclass) = 0.340", abs(cramers_v(t_class) - 0.340) < 0.002)
check("V(Sex) = 0.541", abs(cramers_v(t_sex) - 0.541) < 0.002)
check("3rd class: 24.2% survived, interval 20.7% to 28.2%", abs(g.loc[3, "rate"] - 0.242) < 0.002 and abs(g.loc[3, "lo"] - 0.207) < 0.002 and abs(g.loc[3, "hi"] - 0.282) < 0.002)
**Your answer (1 to 2 sentences).** Both associations have tiny p-values. Which is stronger, and what does that tell you about what a p-value can and cannot say?

## Task 6. Condition on a second variable; Simpson's paradox
**Part A.** Does the class pattern hold *within* each sex? This is a **method chain**: one decision per line. Complete the two blanks in `.agg`.

**Part B: Simpson's paradox**. The Berkeley 1973 admissions data (six largest departments) is provided. Compare the overall rate with the within-department rate.

# Part A: survival by class AND sex (method chain, slide 45)
analysis = (
    df.loc[:, ["Survived", "Pclass", "Sex", "Fare"]]
      .query("Fare >= 0")
      .groupby(["Pclass", "Sex"], observed=True)
      .agg(passengers=("Survived", ___),          # how many rows?
           survival_rate=("Survived", ___),       # the proportion who survived
           median_fare=("Fare", "median"))
      .reset_index()
)
display(analysis.round({"survival_rate": 3, "median_fare": 2}))

male_share = df.groupby("Pclass")["Sex"].apply(lambda s: (s == "male").mean()).round(3)
print("share of men by class:", male_share.to_dict())

# Part B: Simpson's paradox (UC Berkeley 1973)
berk = pd.DataFrame({
    "dept":       list("ABCDEF"),
    "men_apps":   [825, 560, 325, 417, 191, 373],
    "men_adm":    [512, 353, 120, 138,  53,  22],
    "women_apps": [108,  25, 593, 375, 393, 341],
    "women_adm":  [ 89,  17, 202, 131,  94,  24],
})
berk["men_rate"]   = berk["men_adm"] / berk["men_apps"]
berk["women_rate"] = berk["women_adm"] / berk["women_apps"]

overall_men   = ___      # all men admitted / all men who applied
overall_women = ___
n_dept_women_higher = ___   # in how many departments is the women's rate higher?
print(f"overall: men {overall_men:.1%}, women {overall_women:.1%}")
print("departments where women's rate is higher:", n_dept_women_higher, "of 6")
berk.round(3)

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

In `.agg`, the two strings are `"size"` (count rows) and `"mean"` (the mean of a 0/1 column is the proportion). For Part B, the overall rate is the *sum* of admitted divided by the *sum* of applicants. For the last blank: `(berk["women_rate"] > berk["men_rate"]).sum()`.
</details>

check("first-class women: 94 passengers, 96.8% survived", analysis.query("Pclass == 1 and Sex == 'female'")[["passengers", "survival_rate"]].round(3).values.tolist() == [[94, 0.968]])
check("overall: men 44.5%, women 30.4%", abs(overall_men - 0.445) < 0.002 and abs(overall_women - 0.304) < 0.002)
check("women's rate is higher in 4 of 6 departments", n_dept_women_higher == 4)
**Your answer (1 to 2 sentences).** Overall, women were admitted less often, yet within most departments they were admitted *more* often. How can both be true?

## Task 7. Split the data; leak-free scaling with NumPy
**Rule: anything learned from the data (a median, a mean, a standard deviation) must be learned from the training rows only.**

**Part A.** Make a stratified 80/20 split and compare train and test.

**Part B.** Standardise **Age and Fare** with NumPy broadcasting, *using the training rows only*, and apply the same numbers to the test rows.

# Lecture 6 notebook: run the data pipeline demo (in Google Colab or on your own computer)

**Data Handling and Infrastructure for AI | MSc | SETU**

This folder contains a Jupyter notebook, **`Lecture6_Pipeline_Demo_student.ipynb`**, that takes you through the Lecture 6 demo **step by step**. You run a real data pipeline, read its code, test it, break it on purpose, and use it on real Dublin Bikes data.

> **It costs nothing.** You run it in **Google Colab** (free, in your browser, nothing to install) or on your own computer. You do not need a Google Cloud project, credits, or a credit card. (The Google Cloud version is the lab, which comes after.)

**Time:** about 90 to 120 minutes for everything, plus about 5 minutes the first time for the setup in Colab (10 to 20 on your own computer). If you are short of time, do Parts 0 to 5 first: they use only a small sample and need no downloads.

---

## 1. What you will learn

By the end you will be able to:

* explain, in your own words, what a **data pipeline** is and what its parts do;
* read the code of a small Apache Beam pipeline and say what each piece is for;
* run **automatic tests** on a pipeline and understand why they matter;
* read a pipeline's **counters** like a test report, and explain why `rows_read = good rows + bad rows` should always be true;
* explain what a **quarantine** is, and why bad rows are kept with a reason instead of being dropped or crashing the job;
* check a pipeline's result with a **second, independent method** (a reconciliation);
* notice that a published description of a dataset can be **wrong**, and what to do about it.

## 1a. Quick start in Google Colab (recommended)

**Google Colab** is a free service from Google that runs notebooks in your browser. You need only a **Google account**. There is nothing to install: this is the quickest way to start, and it is how the labs are done.

### Open the notebook in Colab (choose one)
* **Option A: one click.** [![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/AbNeil/lecture6_demo/blob/main/lecture6_notebooks/Lecture6_Pipeline_Demo_student.ipynb) This opens the notebook straight from GitHub. (If it says "not found", use Option B.) Colab may warn that the notebook was not written by Google: choose **Run anyway**.
* **Option B: upload the file.** Go to <https://colab.research.google.com>, sign in, choose **File > Upload notebook**, and select `Lecture6_Pipeline_Demo_student.ipynb` (your tutor will give you the file).

### Then
1. **Run the first code cell, "Part 0a".** Click in the cell and press **Shift + Enter**. It downloads the demo code from GitHub and installs Apache Beam. It takes **about a minute**. You should see "Downloading the code from GitHub ... Done." and "Installed."
   * If Colab then asks you to **restart the runtime**, choose **Runtime > Restart session**, then run the Part 0a cell again.
2. **Run the "Part 0" cell.** You should see the folder `/content/lecture6_demo/lecture6_demo` and four version numbers.
3. **Carry on from Part 1,** one cell at a time, in order.

### Things to know about Colab
* **Colab gives you a temporary computer.** If you are idle for a long time, or close the tab, it is **reset**, and everything you created in it is **lost**, including the downloaded data. Nothing is broken: just run the cells again from **Part 0a**.
* **Save your answers.** Use **File > Save a copy in Drive**, or **File > Download > Download .ipynb**, so that your written answers are not lost.
* **Menus have different names from Jupyter:** *Runtime > Restart session* (restart), *Runtime > Run before* (run everything above this cell), *Runtime > Interrupt execution* (stop a cell that never ends).
* **No Google Cloud project, no credits and no GitHub login are needed.** The code repository is public.
* **Colab's computer is shared and not very fast.** The real-data run (Part 6) should still finish in about a minute or two.
* The sections below about a virtual environment, `jupyter lab` and terminals (section 4) are **only for people who run the notebook on their own computer**. In Colab you can ignore them.

---

## 2. What you need on your own computer (not needed in Colab)

| You need | Details |
|---|---|
| A computer | Mac, Windows or Linux. About **1 GB of free disk space** (the libraries are a few hundred MB and the real data is about 130 MB) |
| Python | **Python 3.10, 3.11 or 3.12** (the demo was tested with 3.11 and 3.12). Check yours with `python3 --version` (Mac/Linux) or `py --version` (Windows) |
| Internet | To install the libraries (a few hundred MB) and, in Part 6, to download the real data (about 130 MB) |
| A web browser | Jupyter opens in your browser |
| `git` (optional) | To download the code with one command. Without it you can download a ZIP file instead |

You do **not** need to know Apache Beam, pandas or Jupyter beforehand. The notebook explains what you need as you go.

## 3. What is in the repository

```
lecture6_demo/                     <- the repository (this name appears twice after you clone it)
├── README.md                      <- overview of everything
├── lecture6_demo/                 <- the demo code: the pipeline, its tests, and the scripts
├── lab6_student/                  <- Lab 6 (Google Cloud), later
└── lecture6_notebooks/            <- THIS FOLDER
    ├── README.md                  <- this file
    ├── requirements.txt           <- the libraries to install
    └── Lecture6_Pipeline_Demo_student.ipynb   <- the notebook
```

The notebook finds the demo code in the sibling folder `../lecture6_demo`, so **keep the folders next to each other** and open the notebook from inside `lecture6_notebooks`.

---

## 4. Alternative: set up on your own computer, step by step

**Skip this whole section if you use Colab.** Do this **once**. Take your time: most problems later come from skipping a step here.

### Step 4.1: get the code

**Option A: with git** (recommended). Open a terminal (see 4.2) and run:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/AbNeil/lecture6_demo
cd lecture6_demo
```

**Option B: without git.** Open <https://github.com/AbNeil/lecture6_demo>, click the green **Code** button, choose **Download ZIP**, and unzip it. You will get a folder; open a terminal inside it.

**Option C: from a ZIP file given by your tutor.** Unzip it. If the unzipped folder contains both `lecture6_notebooks` and `lecture6_demo`, you are ready; open a terminal in that folder.

In all cases, the folder you are in must **contain** the two folders `lecture6_demo` and `lecture6_notebooks`. Check with `ls` (Mac/Linux) or `dir` (Windows).

### Step 4.2: open a terminal
* **Mac:** press Cmd + Space, type `Terminal`, press Enter.
* **Windows:** press the Windows key, type `PowerShell`, press Enter. (If you use Anaconda, use **Anaconda Prompt** instead.)
* **Linux:** open your terminal program.

To move into a folder, type `cd` followed by the folder's path. A trick: type `cd ` (with a space), then **drag the folder from your file browser into the terminal window**, and press Enter.

### Step 4.3: create a virtual environment
A **virtual environment** is a private box for this project's Python libraries, so that they do not interfere with anything else on your computer. In the folder from step 4.1:

**Mac / Linux**
```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
```

**Windows (PowerShell)**
```powershell
py -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```
*If PowerShell says "running scripts is disabled", run `Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned`, answer `Y`, and try again. Or use the Command Prompt (`cmd`) and run `.venv\Scripts\activate.bat`.*

When it works, your prompt starts with **`(.venv)`**. **Every time you open a new terminal, you must activate it again** (the second command).

> **Using Anaconda?** Create an environment with `conda create -n lecture6 python=3.11` and `conda activate lecture6`, then continue with step 4.4 (use `pip install` as shown).

### Step 4.4: install the libraries
```bash
cd lecture6_notebooks
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
This installs Apache Beam, pandas, pytest, matplotlib and JupyterLab. **It takes a few minutes** and prints a lot of text. That is normal. It is finished when you get your prompt back without a red `ERROR`.

### Step 4.5: start Jupyter and open the notebook
```bash
jupyter lab
```
Your browser opens (if it does not, copy the address starting `http://localhost:8888/` that appears in the terminal into your browser). In the file list on the left, **double-click `Lecture6_Pipeline_Demo_student.ipynb`**. If asked to choose a kernel, choose **Python 3 (ipykernel)**.

**Leave the terminal window open** while you work: closing it stops Jupyter. To stop Jupyter at the end, press Ctrl + C in the terminal and confirm.

**Using Visual Studio Code instead?** Open the repository folder, install the **Python** and **Jupyter** extensions, open the notebook, click **Select Kernel** (top right) and choose the one named `.venv`.

### Step 4.6: check that it works
Run the first code cell (Part 0). You should see a folder path ending in `lecture6_demo` and four version numbers. If you do, you are ready. If not, see the troubleshooting section below.

---

## 5. How to work through the notebook

* **Run a cell:** click in it and press **Shift + Enter**. Run the cells **in order**.
* **Blanks:** `___` in a code cell means "put your answer here". Until you do, you will get a red `NameError` or `SyntaxError`. That is expected.
* **Checks:** after most tasks a check cell prints **`PASS`** or **`CHECK AGAIN`**. They check numbers, not understanding, so read the explanations too.
* **Hints:** click *Hint* to open it. Try for a couple of minutes first.
* **Written answers:** double-click the cell, write one or two sentences, press Shift + Enter. Nothing is handed in.
* **If you get lost:** Kernel > Restart Kernel, then Run > **Run All Above Selected Cell**.
* **Save often:** Ctrl + S (Cmd + S on a Mac).

## 6. What each part does

| Part | What you do | What you should see |
|---|---|---|
| **0a. Colab setup** | (Colab only) Downloads the demo code from GitHub and installs Apache Beam | "Installed." |
| **0. Setup check** | Finds the demo code and checks the libraries | A folder path and four version numbers |
| **1. Read the code** | Prints each piece of the pipeline, with an explanation, and three small tasks | Three `PASS` lines |
| **2. Tests** | Runs the 5 automatic tests | `5 passed` |
| **3. Sample data** | Creates a small made-up sample (3 files, some deliberately bad rows) and looks inside | 189 lines in total, so 186 data rows |
| **4. Run the sample** | Runs the pipeline locally and reads its counters | `rows_read 186`, `good_rows 182`, `bad_rows 4` and the 4 rejection reasons |
| **5. Exercise 1** | **You** write a CSV with deliberately bad rows, predict the counters, then check | Your prediction matches the real counters |
| **6. Real data** | Downloads real Dublin Bikes data, runs the pipeline, checks it with a second method | About a million rows read, none rejected, two methods agree |
| **7. Exercise 2** | **You** investigate the real results with pandas | Six stations with no name |
| **8. Wrap-up** | Summary, clean-up and glossary | |

### The two exercises

**Exercise 1: break it on purpose (Part 5).** The pipeline has rules about what a good row is. You write a small file containing one row that breaks each rule (a negative number of bikes, an empty station id, an unreadable time, a word instead of a number), one row that is odd but allowed (more bikes than the capacity), and one for an unknown station. **Before running anything you predict** the counters (`rows_read`, `good_rows`, `bad_rows`, `over_capacity`, `unknown_station`). Then you run it and compare. *The aim: understand the rules well enough to predict what happens.* Tip: the over-capacity row is *not* rejected, and `unknown_station` counts hourly **results**, not rows.

**Exercise 2: investigate the real results (Part 7).** In Part 6 a counter called `unknown_station` shows a large number. Using pandas on the pipeline's output you find **which stations** have no name, **when** they appear, and you write down why this might have happened and what you would ask the data owner. *The aim: see that a counter that fires on real data points to a real data problem.*

### About the real data (Part 6)
* The data is published by **Dublin City Council** under the licence **CC BY 4.0** (you may use it with credit): <https://data.smartdublin.ie/dataset/dublinbikes-api>.
* You download **two monthly files** (June 2024 and February 2026) and a station list: about **130 MB** in total.
* **Slow connection or no internet in the lab?** Ask your tutor for the files. They must end up in `lecture6_demo/data/raw/` (two CSV files) and `lecture6_demo/data/ref/dublin.csv`.
* If you want to skip the real data for now, set `RUN_REAL = False` in the Part 6 cell. Everything real then skips itself.
* The numbers in the notebook (such as 1,052,292 rows) are for the files as they were when the lecture was written. If the council updates a file, your numbers may differ a little: tell your tutor, and do not worry.

---

## 7. Troubleshooting

Find your message in the left column.

| What you see | What it means and what to do |
|---|---|
| **In Colab:** `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'apache_beam'` | Run the **Part 0a** cell. If Colab asks to restart, do **Runtime > Restart session**, then run Part 0a and Part 0 again |
| **In Colab:** `fatal: unable to access 'https://github.com/...'` | Colab cannot reach GitHub right now. Wait a minute and run the Part 0a cell again. If it keeps failing, tell your tutor |
| **In Colab:** everything I made has disappeared | Colab reset your temporary computer (idle for a long time, or the tab was closed). Run the cells again from Part 0a. To keep your answers next time, save a copy (File > Save a copy in Drive) |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'apache_beam'` (or `pandas`, `matplotlib`, `pytest`) **on your own computer, in the notebook** | The notebook is using a different Python from the one you installed into. In JupyterLab: **Kernel > Change Kernel** and choose the kernel with `.venv` in its name. If it is not listed: stop Jupyter (Ctrl + C), activate the environment (step 4.3), run `jupyter lab` from the `lecture6_notebooks` folder again |
| The same error **in the terminal** while installing | Your environment is not active. Look for `(.venv)` at the start of the prompt; if it is missing, activate it (step 4.3) and run the install again |
| `I cannot find bike_pipeline.py` | **In Colab:** run the Part 0a cell first. **On your own computer:** the notebook is not in the right place. It must be in `lecture6_notebooks`, next to the `lecture6_demo` folder. Check with `ls` / `dir` in the folder that contains both |
| `pip install` fails with a long red error | Check `python3 --version`: Apache Beam needs a supported Python (3.10 to 3.12 were tested). Newer versions may not work yet. ## Part 1. Read the pipeline's code (15 min)

A **data pipeline** is an automated, repeatable series of steps that moves data from where it is produced to where it is used, checking and transforming it on the way. Ours does five things:

```
CSV files ──► read each file ──► check every row ──┬─ good rows ──► hourly windows ──► averages per station ──► add station name ──► results
                                                    └─ bad rows  ──► quarantine (with the reason) ───────────────────────────────────► rejected rows
```

Its question is simple: **for each bike station and each hour, how many bikes were available on average, at least, and at most?**

The code is in `bike_pipeline.py`. We load it into this notebook and print its parts, with an explanation of each. **Read the code, then the explanation next to it.** You do not need to memorise any of it.

### Piece 1: reading one file (`ReadCsvFile`)
Run the cell, then read the notes under it.
show(bp.ReadCsvFile)

**What to notice**
1. A `DoFn` is a class with a `process` method. For each input it may produce any number of outputs (here: one per row).
2. The input is a **whole file**, not a row. That lets us read **that file's own header** with `csv.DictReader`. Each row becomes a dictionary like `{"station_id": "42", "num_bikes_available": "5", ...}`, so we find columns **by name, never by position**. This matters because files can have different columns.
3. `utf-8-sig` quietly removes an invisible marker that some CSV files start with.
4. `row["_source"] = name` remembers which file each row came from, so a problem can be traced back.
5. The **counters** (`files_read`, `rows_read`, `empty_files`) are how the pipeline reports what happened. An empty file gives zero rows and is counted, not crashed on.
### Piece 2: reading times and numbers safely

show(bp.RowError)
show(bp.parse_timestamp)
show(bp.to_int)

**What to notice**
1. `RowError` is our own kind of error. Its message is the **reason** a row is rejected.
2. `parse_timestamp` accepts either a number of seconds since 1970 or text such as `2024-06-01 00:05:00`. If the text has **no time zone** (as in the real files), we **assume UTC**. That is an assumption about the data, and a good pipeline says so.
3. `to_int` accepts `12` and `12.0` but turns anything else (such as `"many"`) into a `RowError` with a reason that names the column.
### Piece 3: the data contract as code (`ValidateRow`)
show(bp.ValidateRow)

**What to notice**
1. This is the **data contract** from Lecture 5, now running on every row. In order, it checks: the three required columns are present and not empty; the station and the bike count are whole numbers; the time can be read; the bike count is not negative.
2. A row that breaks a rule is **not dropped silently and does not crash the job**. It goes to a second output, named `BAD`, together with the reason, the file name and the raw row. That is the **quarantine**.
3. `over_capacity` is a *plausibility* rule: more bikes than the station's capacity is odd but possible, so we **keep** the row and just **count** it (Lecture 5: flag, do not delete).
### Piece 4: how the averages are computed (`BikeStats`)
show(bp.BikeStats)

**What to notice**
1. A `CombineFn` computes an aggregate in four small steps so that many machines can share the work: start empty (`create_accumulator`), add one reading (`add_input`), join partial results from different machines (`merge_accumulators`), and produce the answer (`extract_output`).
2. We carry the **total and the count**, not the average itself, because two averages cannot be merged correctly without knowing how many readings each came from.

### Piece 5: the whole pipeline in one place (`build`)
This is the most important piece. Read it **top to bottom**: every line is one step, written `| "Name" >> step`.
show(bp.build)

**What to notice**
* `stations` is a small side branch: it reads the station reference file (number and name).
* `checked` finds the files (`MatchFiles`), opens them (`ReadMatches`), reads their rows (`ReadRows`) and validates them (`Validate`), with **two outputs**: `good` and the `BAD` quarantine.
* `hourly` continues with the good rows: `Stamp` (give each reading its real time), `Hourly` (cut time into windows), `Stats` (average, minimum, maximum per station and window), and `Enrich` (add the station name from the side input).

def run_pipeline(input_glob, stations, output_prefix, extra=()):
    """Run bike_pipeline.py locally. Returns (exit code, counters as a dict, seconds taken)."""
    args = [PY, "bike_pipeline.py", "--runner", "DirectRunner", "--input", input_glob,
            "--stations", stations, "--output", output_prefix, *extra]
    start = time.time()
    code, out = run(args)
    counters = {m.group(1): int(m.group(2)) for m in re.finditer(r"^\s{2}(\w+)\s+(\d+)\s*$", out, flags=re.M)}
    return code, counters, time.time() - start

def read_jsonl(pattern):
    """Read all the result files that match a pattern into one table."""
    frames = [pd.read_json(f, lines=True) for f in sorted(glob.glob(pattern)) if os.path.getsize(f) > 0]
    return pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True) if frames else pd.DataFrame()

### Five ideas to remember
1. **Look at the data before you run anything on it.**
2. **Count every row**: `rows_read = good + bad`, always.
3. **Quarantine, do not crash and do not hide.**
4. **A description of a dataset is not the data** (the web page was wrong twice).

### Glossary
| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Pipeline | The steps that take raw data to a trustworthy result, automatically |
| Apache Beam | The programming model (and Python library) used to write the pipeline |
| DirectRunner | Beam's runner that works on your own computer |
| PCollection | A dataset inside the pipeline |
| DoFn | A class that defines one step, with a `process` method |
| Counter | A number the pipeline keeps to report what happened |
| Quarantine | Where rows that break the rules are kept, with the reason |
| Window | A slice of time (here, one hour) used to group readings |
| Data contract | The rules the data must follow, written as code |
| Reconciliation | Checking that two different methods give the same answer |
| Schema drift | The columns of a file changing over time |
